title: Sudoku, and Where Plain Backtracking Runs Out
excerpt: The problem where choosing which decision to make next matters more than the algorithm around it. One change to the cell ordering takes the solver from 56 dead ends to none.

content.text: Sudoku is the problem where the choice of
which decision to make next
matters more than anything else in the algorithm. The rules are simple, the template is the one you already know, and a single change to the ordering makes the solver about four times cheaper.

Before the algorithm, a framing worth carrying. Make each of the 81 cells a node. Join two cells with an edge when they share a row, a column or a 3 by 3 box, meaning they are not allowed to hold the same digit. Now solving the puzzle is coloring that graph with 9 colors, where some nodes arrive pre-colored.

The similarity runs deeper than a comparison. Coloring a graph and solving a puzzle board are the same search wearing different labels, which is why the previous page's algorithm works here with almost no modification. It also sets expectations: coloring is hard in general, so do not expect a formula.
The obvious way to pick the next blank is reading order: top-left to bottom-right. It is simple and there is nothing wrong with it except that it ignores information sitting in plain view.

Consider a blank with 6 legal digits and another with 1. Filling the 6-candidate cell means branching six ways, and if the puzzle is doomed from here you will discover that six times over. Filling the 1-candidate cell means branching once, and the digit is forced, so no guess is being made at all.
So a better rule: always fill the blank with the fewest legal digits remaining. This is called the
most constrained variable
heuristic, and versions of it appear across the whole of constraint solving.

Two things happen at once. Forced cells get filled immediately and for free, which is exactly what a human solver does. And when a guess is genuinely required, it is made where the branching factor is smallest, so a wrong guess is discovered after the least possible work.
On the puzzle bundled with the widget below, the two orderings differ like this.

The only difference is which blank the solver picks next.

content.text: Read the dead-ends column again. The most-constrained ordering hit
zero

dead ends. It never guessed wrong, not because it was lucky, but because it kept choosing cells where the answer was already determined, and by the time a real choice was needed the grid had enough information to make it safely.

Nothing about the rules changed. No prune was added. The solver simply asked its questions in a better order, which is a genuinely different kind of optimization from the ones earlier in this section and often the most powerful one available.
Switch between the two orderings and watch the counters, since the finished grid is identical either way.
The solver itself is the template unchanged, and everything interesting has moved into pickCell.
The early return when a cell has exactly one candidate is a small but real saving. No cell can be better than forced, so there is no point scanning the remaining blanks once you have found one.
Two more ideas turn this into something that handles the puzzles marketed as impossible.

The first is constraint propagation. After placing a digit, update the candidate lists of every cell that sees it. If any cell drops to zero candidates, the branch is dead immediately rather than several placements later. If any drops to one, fill it at once and propagate again. Much of a hard puzzle solves itself this way with no guessing at all.

The second is the least-constraining value: among the digits legal for the chosen cell, try first the one that removes the fewest options from its neighbors. Choose the cell that constrains you most, then the value that constrains you least. That pairing is the standard shape of a good constraint solver.
Recomputing candidate counts from scratch on every call.
Correct, and it can cost more than the search it saves on large grids. Keep the counts updated as cells are filled and cleared.
Forgetting the box check.
Row and column are easy to remember and the 3 by 3 box is easy to leave out. The solver then produces grids that look almost right and violate the rule everyone checks last.
Not undoing on failure.
The same bug as everywhere else, and here it leaves stale digits that make later branches appear illegal, so the solver reports an unsolvable puzzle that is perfectly solvable.
Assuming one solution exists.

A proper Sudoku has exactly one. A puzzle with too few givens has many, and a solver that stops at the first will happily return one of them. If uniqueness matters, keep searching after the first success and count.

questions.prompt: Why does filling the most constrained cell first help so much?

options.label: It minimizes branching where guesses are needed, and fills forced cells with no guess at all
It fills the grid in fewer total placements
It makes the legality check cheaper

questions.prompt: The most-constrained solver hit zero dead ends on the sample puzzle. What does that mean?

options.label: It never had to undo a placement, because each choice was already determined or safe when made
The puzzle had only one blank cell
It found a different solution from the naive version

questions.prompt: How is Sudoku the same problem as graph coloring?

options.label: Cells are nodes, edges join cells that may not match, and the 9 digits are the colors
Both are solved by breadth-first search
Both require exactly nine colors for any input

questions.prompt: What is constraint propagation, in one sentence?

options.label: After placing a digit, update every affected cell's candidates and act immediately on any that reach zero or one
Trying every digit in every cell before recursing
Sorting the cells by how many givens surround them

seoTitle: Sudoku Solver with Backtracking: Cell Ordering and Constraint Propagation
seoDescription: Sudoku as backtracking: why it is graph coloring in disguise, the most-constrained-variable heuristic and the numbers behind it, constraint propagation, and the bugs that make a solvable grid look unsolvable.
